Kennungen mit Präfix c1-, nie ändern: sie stehen in grammar/<id>. Der Claude-Tagesauftrag nutzt weiter nur die 16 alten Kennungen.

topics.name: Hedging – abschwächen und absichern
topics.rule: Aussagen vorsichtig formulieren: Modalverben („might“, „could“, „may“), Einleitungen („It might be worth …“, „I'd be inclined to …“, „It seems that …“) und Weichmacher („a bit“, „slightly“, „somewhat“). So bleiben Bewertungen offen und glaubwürdig.
topics.rule_en: Make statements tentative: modal verbs (might, could, may), lead-ins (It might be worth …, I'd be inclined to …, It seems that …) and softeners (a bit, slightly, somewhat). This keeps judgments open and credible.
ex: It might be worth considering a phased rollout.
I'd be inclined to start with the finance team.

topics.name: Diplomatische Distanz
topics.rule: Bitten und Einwände mit Abstand formulieren: Vergangenheit und Verlaufsform („I was wondering whether …“, „We were hoping …“), Fragen statt Aufforderungen („Would it be possible to …?“) und Untertreibung („That could be tricky for us.“). Die Vergangenheit meint hier keine Zeit, sie macht die Bitte höflicher.
topics.rule_en: Phrase requests and objections with distance: past and continuous forms (“I was wondering whether …”, “We were hoping …”), questions instead of orders (“Would it be possible to …?”) and understatement (“That could be tricky for us.”). The past tense here is not about time, it makes the request more polite.
ex: I was wondering whether you could share the requirements by Friday.
That could be a bit tricky for us.

topics.name: Betonung durch Satzbau (Cleft, Inversion)
topics.rule: Cleft-Sätze heben einen Teil hervor: „What we really need is …“, „It was the CFO who …“. Inversion nach einschränkenden Wörtern am Satzanfang (Not only, Never, Rarely, Only after) stellt das Hilfsverb vor das Subjekt: „Not only did we cut costs, but we also …“.
topics.rule_en: Cleft sentences put one part in the spotlight: “What we really need is …”, “It was the CFO who …”. Inversion after limiting words at the start (Not only, Never, Rarely, Only after) puts the auxiliary before the subject: “Not only did we cut costs, but we also …”.
ex: What we really need is a clear timeline.
Not only did we cut costs, but we also improved compliance.

topics.name: Diskursmarker
topics.rule: Diskursmarker führen den Zuhörer: einschränken (That said, Having said that), anknüpfen (To build on that), zurückkommen (Coming back to …), gegenüberstellen (On the other hand), zusammenfassen (In short, All in all). Sie stehen meist am Satzanfang, gefolgt von einem Komma.
topics.rule_en: Discourse markers guide the listener: qualify (That said, Having said that), build on (To build on that), return (Coming back to …), contrast (On the other hand), sum up (In short, All in all). They usually start the sentence, followed by a comma.
ex: That said, the timeline is still tight.
To build on that, we could add e-invoicing in phase two.

topics.name: Nominalstil in Mails
topics.rule: Nominalstil verdichtet Mails: statt vieler Nebensätze ein Nomen mit „of“ („the implementation of the new archive“). Typische Paare: implement → implementation, approve → approval, migrate → migration, decide → decision, deliver → delivery, receive → receipt. Sparsam einsetzen – zu viele Nomen machen Mails steif.
topics.rule_en: Nominal style condenses emails: instead of several clauses, one noun with “of” (“the implementation of the new archive”). Typical pairs: implement → implementation, approve → approval, migrate → migration, decide → decision, deliver → delivery, receive → receipt. Use it sparingly – too many nouns make emails stiff.
ex: The implementation of the archive starts in May.
Following the approval of the budget, we will order the licenses.

topics.name: Partizipialsätze
topics.rule: Partizipialsätze verkürzen Nebensätze mit demselben Subjekt: Having + 3. Form für etwas vorher Abgeschlossenes („Having reviewed the contract, we …“), -ing für Gleichzeitiges („Using OCR, the system …“), 3. Form für Passiv („Stored in Germany, the data …“). Das Subjekt des Hauptsatzes muss zum Partizip passen.
topics.rule_en: Participle clauses shorten clauses with the same subject: Having + past participle for something completed before (“Having reviewed the contract, we …”), -ing for something at the same time (“Using OCR, the system …”), past participle for passive (“Stored in Germany, the data …”). The subject of the main clause must match the participle.
ex: Having reviewed the contract, we signed it.
Stored in Germany, the data stays GDPR-compliant.

topics.name: Präzise Mengen- und Zeitangaben
topics.rule: Präzise statt vage: Mengen mit roughly, just under, well over, a fraction of, twice as … as; Zeiten mit by the end of Q3, within two weeks, as of June 1, no later than Friday. by = spätestens bis, until = durchgehend bis, within = innerhalb von.
topics.rule_en: Precise instead of vague: quantities with roughly, just under, well over, a fraction of, twice as … as; time with by the end of Q3, within two weeks, as of June 1, no later than Friday. by = at the latest, until = all the way up to, within = inside a period.
ex: Roughly 40% of the invoices arrive as PDFs.
We need your decision by the end of Q3.

topics.name: Zeitsätze – when, as soon as, until, by the time
topics.name_en: Time clauses: when, as soon as, until, by the time
topics.rule: Nach when, as soon as, until, before, after und by the time steht bei Zukünftigem das Präsens (oder das Present Perfect), nie „will“. „By the time“ führt oft zu will have + Partizip im Hauptsatz.
topics.rule_en: After when, as soon as, until, before, after and by the time, use the present tense (or present perfect) for future meaning, never will. “By the time” often goes with will have + participle in the main clause.
ex: I'll call you as soon as the shipment arrives.
We won't sign until the legal team has approved the draft.

topics.name: Bedingungen mit unless, as long as, provided that
topics.name_en: Conditionals beyond if: unless, as long as, provided that
topics.rule: „Unless“ heißt „wenn nicht“, „as long as“ und „provided that“ heißen „solange / unter der Bedingung, dass“. Nach diesen drei Wörtern steht kein „will“. „But for“ meint „ohne“ im Rückblick; „Should you …“ ist die förmliche Form ohne if. „Otherwise“ ersetzt kein if: Es heißt „sonst“ und beginnt einen neuen Satz.
topics.rule_en: “Unless” means “if not”, “as long as” and “provided that” mean “on condition that”. After these three words there is no will. “But for” means “without” in hindsight; “Should you …” is the formal form without if. “Otherwise” does not replace if: it means “or else” and starts a new sentence.
ex: We'll miss the deadline unless we hire extra staff.
You can use the car as long as you return it by Friday.

topics.name: Passiv erweitert – Modalverben, Perfekt, -ing, „is said to“
topics.name_en: Passive extended: modals, perfect, -ing, “is said to”
topics.rule: Das Passiv gibt es auch mit Modalverben (must be signed), im Perfekt (has been signed), als Gerundium (being asked) und als persönliche Konstruktion („The CEO is said to have resigned“). So bleibt der Handelnde unwichtig oder unbekannt.
topics.rule_en: The passive also works with modals (must be signed), in the perfect (has been signed), as a gerund (being asked) and in personal constructions (“The CEO is said to have resigned”). The doer stays unimportant or unknown.
ex: The contract must be signed before Friday.
The company is said to have lost millions last year.

topics.name: Berichtsverben – suggest, admit, insist, advise, recommend
topics.name_en: Reporting verbs: suggest, admit, insist, advise, recommend
topics.rule: Jedes Berichtsverb hat sein festes Muster: suggest / recommend + -ing oder that-Satz, admit / deny + -ing, insist on + -ing, advise / warn + Person + to-Infinitiv. Man darf die Muster nicht mischen.
topics.rule_en: Each reporting verb has its own pattern: suggest / recommend + -ing or that-clause, admit / deny + -ing, insist on + -ing, advise / warn + person + to-infinitive. The patterns cannot be mixed.
ex: She suggested moving the meeting to Thursday.
My lawyer advised me not to sign the document.

topics.name: Fragen – indirekte Fragen, Frageanhängsel, Subjektfragen
topics.name_en: Questions: indirect questions, question tags, subject questions
topics.rule: In indirekten Fragen steht normale Satzstellung (Could you tell me where the room is?). Frageanhängsel kehren die Polarität um (isn't it?). Fragt man nach dem Subjekt, steht kein „do“ (Who called?).
topics.rule_en: In indirect questions use normal word order (Could you tell me where the room is?). Question tags reverse the polarity (isn't it?). Subject questions use no do (Who called?).
ex: Could you tell me where the finance department is?
Who called me while I was in the meeting?

topics.name: Modalverben für Ratschläge – should, ought to, had better, need to
topics.name_en: Modals for advice: should, ought to, had better, need to
topics.rule: „Should“ und „ought to“ raten freundlich, „had better“ warnt mit Folgen, „must“ und „have to“ drücken Pflicht aus, „don't have to“ heißt „nicht nötig“. Im Beruf wählt man die Stärke nach Rolle und Höflichkeit.
topics.rule_en: “Should” and “ought to” advise gently, “had better” warns with consequences, “must” and “have to” express obligation, “don't have to” means “not necessary”. At work you choose strength by role and politeness.
ex: You should call the client before noon.
You had better tell your manager today.

topics.name: Verb + to-Infinitiv oder -ing
topics.rule: Manche Verben ändern ihre Bedeutung je nach Form: remember doing = sich erinnern, dass man etwas tat; remember to do = daran denken. Ebenso stop, try und regret. Nach look forward to, avoid und mind steht immer -ing.
topics.rule_en: Some verbs change meaning with the form: remember doing = recall having done; remember to do = not forget. The same holds for stop, try and regret. After look forward to, avoid and mind always use -ing.
ex: Please remember to send the report before you leave.
I look forward to meeting you at the conference.

topics.name: Mandativ-Subjunctiv – suggest that he be …
topics.name_en: The mandative subjunctive: insist that he be …
topics.rule: Nach Verben wie suggest, insist, demand, recommend und Ausdrücken wie „It is essential / vital / important that“ steht im formellen (US-)Englisch die Grundform: „I suggest that she call“, „It is essential that he be present“.
topics.rule_en: After verbs like suggest, insist, demand, recommend and phrases like “It is essential / vital / important that”, formal (US) English uses the base form: “I suggest that she call”, “It is essential that he be present”.
ex: The board insists that he leave the project immediately.
It is essential that every employee complete the training.

topics.name: Zählbar und unzählbar
topics.rule: „advice“, „information“, „feedback“ und „furniture“ sind unzählbar: kein „-s“, kein „a/an“, dazu „much“, „a little“, „some“. Zählbares nimmt „many“ und „a few“.
topics.rule_en: “Advice”, “information”, “feedback” and “furniture” are uncountable: no -s, no a/an, but much, a little, some. Countable nouns take many and a few.
ex: I need some information about the contract.
How many meetings do we have this week?

topics.name: Präpositionen nach Nomen und Adjektiv
topics.rule: Viele Nomen und Adjektive haben eine feste Präposition: „reason for“, „increase in“, „interested in“, „responsible for“. Sie lässt sich selten wörtlich aus dem Deutschen ableiten.
topics.rule_en: Many nouns and adjectives take a fixed preposition: reason for, increase in, interested in, responsible for. It can rarely be translated literally from German.
ex: There was a sharp increase in demand.
She is responsible for the Munich office.

topics.name: Zeitpräpositionen
topics.rule: „at“ für Uhrzeiten, „on“ für Tage, „in“ für Monate und Jahre. „for“ nennt die Dauer, „since“ den Beginn; „by“ ist die Frist, „until“ der Endpunkt, „within“ der Zeitrahmen.
topics.rule_en: “At” for clock times, “on” for days, “in” for months and years. “For” gives the duration, “since” the start; “by” is a deadline, “until” an end point, “within” a time frame.
ex: Please reply by Friday at the latest.
We've worked together since 2020.

topics.name: Zusammengesetzte Modifikatoren und Adjektivreihenfolge
topics.rule: Vor dem Nomen stehen Maße im Singular mit Bindestrich: „a 10-page report“. Mehrere Adjektive folgen einer festen Reihenfolge: Meinung, Größe, Alter, Farbe, Herkunft, Stoff.
topics.rule_en: Before a noun, measurements stay singular with a hyphen: “a 10-page report”. Several adjectives follow a fixed order: opinion, size, age, color, origin, material.
ex: We signed a three-year contract.
She bought a new black German laptop.

topics.name: Phrasal Verbs: Stellung
topics.rule: Bei trennbaren Phrasal Verbs steht ein Pronomen immer in der Mitte: „look it over“. Untrennbare und Drei-Wort-Verben bleiben zusammen: „look forward to“, „put up with“.
topics.rule_en: With separable phrasal verbs, a pronoun always goes in the middle: “look it over”. Inseparable and three-word verbs stay together: “look forward to”, “put up with”.
ex: Could you look it over before we send it?
I can't put up with these delays.

topics.name: Satzstellung und Inversion
topics.rule: Ort steht meist vor Zeit („in Munich tomorrow“). Nach verneinenden Einleitungen wie „never“, „rarely“, „not only“ folgt die Frage-Stellung: „Rarely have we seen …“.
topics.rule_en: Place usually comes before time (“in Munich tomorrow”). After negative openers like never, rarely and not only, question word order follows: “Rarely have we seen …”.
ex: Never have we seen such a strong response.
We will meet in Berlin next week.

topics.name: Konnektoren: Satzbau und Zeichensetzung
topics.rule: „although“ steht vor einem Satz, „despite/in spite of“ vor Nomen oder -ing. „however“ und „therefore“ brauchen Punkt oder Semikolon davor und Komma danach, „whereas“ und „while“ verbinden Gegensätze.
topics.rule_en: “Although” goes before a clause, “despite/in spite of” before a noun or -ing. “However” and “therefore” need a period or semicolon before and a comma after; “whereas” and “while” link contrasts.
ex: Although it was late, we kept working.
Sales rose; however, profits fell.

topics.name: Vergleiche
topics.rule: „the more … the more“ verknüpft zwei Entwicklungen. „as … as“ drückt Gleichheit aus, „than“ den Unterschied. „far“, „much“ und „slightly“ verstärken oder mildern den Komparativ.
topics.rule_en: “The more … the more” links two developments. “As … as” expresses equality, “than” a difference. “Far”, “much” and “slightly” strengthen or soften the comparative.
ex: The more we practice, the better we get.
Their offer is slightly cheaper than ours.

topics.name: Inversion – Umstellung nach Einleitern
topics.rule: Steht ein verneinendes oder einschränkendes Wort vorn (Never, Rarely, Only after, No sooner, Should you), kommt das Hilfsverb vor das Subjekt: „Rarely have we seen such a plan.“ So klingt eine Aussage förmlich und betont.
topics.rule_en: When a negative or limiting word comes first (Never, Rarely, Only after, No sooner, Should you), the auxiliary goes before the subject: “Rarely have we seen such a plan.” This makes a statement formal and emphatic.
ex: Never before had the team met a deadline so early.
Should you need any help, please let us know.

topics.name: Hervorheben mit do und Voranstellung
topics.rule: Mit do („I do think“), einem vorangestellten Adjektiv („Tempting as it is“), so/such … that und einem vorgezogenen Objekt („This we must avoid“) hebst du Wichtiges hervor, ohne laut zu werden.
topics.rule_en: With do (“I do think”), a fronted adjective (“Tempting as it is”), so/such … that and a fronted object (“This we must avoid”) you stress what matters without raising your voice.
ex: We did send the invoice last week; please check your spam folder.
Much as I would like to help, I cannot approve this.

topics.name: Ellipse – Wiederholung vermeiden
topics.rule: Was schon gesagt ist, lässt man weg oder ersetzt es: „I think so“, „we did so“, „the new one“, „those of the old plan“, „I’d love to“. So klingt Englisch knapp und natürlich.
topics.rule_en: What has already been said is left out or replaced: “I think so”, “we did so”, “the new one”, “those of the old plan”, “I’d love to”. This makes English sound short and natural.
ex: Will the update be ready on Friday? I think so.
The costs of the new plan are lower than those of the old one.

topics.name: Nominalgruppen – das Nomen ausbauen
topics.name_en: Noun phrases: building around the noun
topics.rule: Um ein Nomen herum baut man Information auf: einen Satz ohne that („the system we tested“), ein Partizip („the files stored in the cloud“), ’s oder of („the manager’s decision“) und einen to-Infinitiv („the first to sign“).
topics.rule_en: You build information around a noun: a clause without that (“the system we tested”), a participle (“the files stored in the cloud”), ’s or of (“the manager’s decision”) and a to-infinitive (“the first to sign”).
ex: This is the most reliable system we have tested.
She was the first customer to sign the new contract.

topics.name: Wahrscheinlichkeit mit Modalverben
topics.rule: Wie wahrscheinlich etwas ist, sagst du in Stufen: „may well“ (durchaus möglich), „is likely to“ (wahrscheinlich), „is bound to“ (so gut wie sicher) und „There is a good chance that …“.
topics.rule_en: You express how probable something is in steps: “may well” (quite possible), “is likely to” (probable), “is bound to” (almost certain) and “There is a good chance that …”.
ex: The client may well reject the first offer.
Prices are bound to rise after the merger.

topics.name: Verlaufsform mit Zustandsverben
topics.rule: Die Verlaufsform zeigt Wandel, Höflichkeit und Verhalten: „We are seeing growth“, „I was hoping you could help“, „You are being difficult“. Reine Zustände wie know, need oder belong stehen dagegen in der einfachen Form.
topics.rule_en: The continuous shows change, politeness and behavior: “We are seeing growth”, “I was hoping you could help”, “You are being difficult”. Pure states like know, need or belong stay in the simple form.
ex: We are seeing a clear rise in demand.
I was hoping you could review the draft.

topics.name: Zukunft in der Vergangenheit
topics.rule: Wenn du aus der Vergangenheit auf etwas Späteres blickst, ändern sich die Formen: „was going to“ (Plan), „was about to“ (gerade im Begriff), „would“ (später geschah) und „was to“ (vorgesehen). Häufig ging der Plan nicht auf.
topics.rule_en: When you look from the past at something later, the forms change: “was going to” (plan), “was about to” (on the point of), “would” (later happened) and “was to” (meant to). Often the plan did not work out.
ex: We were going to launch in May, but the supplier was late.
She joined in 2015 and would later lead the Berlin office.

topics.name: Verneinung und Mengen
topics.rule: Verneinung und Mengen haben feste Formen: „none of“ und „neither of“ für „keiner“, „hardly“ und „scarcely“ für „kaum“ (schon verneint), „no longer“ für „nicht mehr“ und „a number of“ gegen „the number of“.
topics.rule_en: Negation and quantity have fixed forms: “none of” and “neither of” for “not one”, “hardly” and “scarcely” for “barely” (already negative), “no longer” for “not anymore” and “a number of” versus “the number of”.
ex: None of the suppliers has replied yet.
We no longer offer this service.

core: Mit vorsichtigen Wörtern klingt eine Aussage weicher und höflicher: might/could/may, „It might be worth + -ing“, „I’d be inclined to …“ und Abschwächer wie „a bit“. Beispiel: „The price might be a bit above our budget.“

Careful words make a statement sound softer and more polite: might/could/may, “It might be worth + -ing”, “I’d be inclined to …” and softeners like “a bit”. Example: “The price might be a bit above our budget.”
why: Absolute Aussagen wirken im Englischen schnell arrogant oder angreifbar. Wer abschwächt, lässt dem Gegenüber Raum – und bleibt glaubwürdig, wenn sich Zahlen später ändern.
Absolute statements quickly sound arrogant or easy to attack in English. Hedging leaves the other person room – and keeps you credible if the numbers change later.
contrast: Auf Deutsch gilt Direktheit als ehrlich („Das ist zu teuer.“). Auf Englisch klingt derselbe Satz schroff; üblich ist „That might be a bit above our budget.“
In German, directness sounds honest (“Das ist zu teuer.”). In English the same sentence sounds blunt; people say “That might be a bit above our budget.”
steps: Ist es eine Vermutung oder Bewertung? Dann abschwächen.
Modalverb wählen: might, could oder may statt will oder is.
Bei Bedarf einen Weichmacher ergänzen: a bit, slightly, somewhat.
Nicht übertreiben: Eine Abschwächung pro Satz reicht.
Is it a guess or a judgment? Then soften it.
Choose a modal: might, could or may instead of will or is.
Add a softener if needed: a bit, slightly, somewhat.
Don't overdo it: one hedge per sentence is enough.
forms: It might be worth revisiting the timeline.
I'd be inclined to + base form
I'd be inclined to start with a pilot.
It seems that the budget is tighter than expected.

traps.bad: It might be worth to wait until Q3.
traps.good: It might be worth waiting until Q3.
why: Nach „worth“ steht immer die -ing-Form.
“Worth” is always followed by the -ing form.

core: Höfliche Bitten klingen indirekter: „I was wondering whether …“, „We were hoping …“, „Would it be possible to …?“. Auch Untertreibung hilft: „That’s not ideal“ statt „That’s bad.“
Polite requests sound more indirect: “I was wondering whether …”, “We were hoping …”, “Would it be possible to …?”. Understatement helps too: “That’s not ideal” instead of “That’s bad.”
why: Je weiter eine Bitte grammatisch von „jetzt“ und „du musst“ entfernt ist, desto höflicher klingt sie. So kann das Gegenüber ablehnen, ohne das Gesicht zu verlieren – im Vertrieb Gold wert.
The further a request moves away from “now” and “you must”, the more polite it sounds. The other person can say no without losing face – invaluable in sales.
contrast: Auf Deutsch ist „Können Sie mir bis Freitag die Daten schicken?“ völlig höflich. Wörtlich übersetzt („Can you send me the data by Friday?“) wirkt es auf Englisch fast wie eine Anweisung.
In German, “Können Sie mir bis Freitag die Daten schicken?” is perfectly polite. Translated word for word, it can sound almost like an order in English.
steps: Anweisung oder Einwand? Dann Abstand schaffen.
Vergangenheit wählen: I was wondering, We were hoping.
Im Rest des Satzes bleibt der Abstand: could statt can.
Einwände untertreiben: tricky, a challenge, not ideal.
An order or an objection? Then create distance.
Use the past: I was wondering, We were hoping.
Keep the distance in the rest of the sentence: could instead of can.
Understate objections: tricky, a challenge, not ideal.
forms: I was wondering whether we could move the call.
We were hoping to + base form
We were hoping to sign before the end of Q3.
Would it be possible to + base form?
Would it be possible to extend the trial?
That could be tricky / a challenge for us.
That could be a challenge for us.

traps.bad: Would it be possible that you send the offer again?
traps.good: Would it be possible to send the offer again?
why: Nach „Would it be possible“ folgt to + Grundform, kein „that“-Satz.
“Would it be possible” is followed by to + base form, not a that-clause.

core: Mit besonderen Satzformen betonst du einen Teil des Satzes: „What we need is more time.“ (What-Satz), „It was the client who called.“ (It-Satz) oder „Not only did we finish, …“ (Umstellung nach Wörtern wie not only).

Special sentence patterns stress one part of the sentence: “What we need is more time.” (what-cleft), “It was the client who called.” (it-cleft) or “Not only did we finish, …” (inversion after words like not only).
why: Im Englischen kann man kaum mit der Stimme allein betonen, ohne dramatisch zu wirken. Der Satzbau übernimmt das: Was vorne im Cleft steht, wird zur Hauptsache. Inversion klingt souverän und präsentationsreif.

In English you can hardly stress words with your voice alone without sounding dramatic. Sentence structure does the job: whatever you put in the cleft becomes the main point. Inversion sounds confident and ready for a presentation.
contrast: Deutsch betont oft durch Umstellen („Genau das brauchen wir.“). Englisch hat eine feste Wortstellung und braucht dafür eigene Bauformen. Nach „Not only“ am Satzanfang muss wie in einer Frage das Hilfsverb vor das Subjekt – das vergessen Deutsche oft.

German often stresses by moving words around. English has a fixed word order and needs special structures for that. After “Not only” at the start, the auxiliary must come before the subject, as in a question – German speakers often forget this.
steps: Was soll betont werden? Das kommt in den Fokus.
Sache betonen: What + Subjekt + Verb + is …
Person oder Ding betonen: It was X who/that …
Einschränkendes Wort am Anfang? Dann Hilfsverb vor das Subjekt (do/did, have, can …).
What should be stressed? That goes into focus.
Stress a thing: What + subject + verb + is …
Stress a person or item: It was X who/that …
Limiting word at the start? Then put the auxiliary before the subject (do/did, have, can …).
forms: What we really need is a clear timeline.
It is / was + X + who / that …
It was the CFO who approved the budget.
Not only + aux + S + V …, but S also …
Not only did we cut costs, but we also improved compliance.
Rarely have we seen such a fast rollout.
signals: Not only / Never / Rarely / Only after …
puts the thing in the spotlight

traps.bad: Not only we reduced the costs, but we also sped up approvals.
traps.good: Not only did we reduce the costs, but we also sped up approvals.
why: Nach „Not only“ am Satzanfang steht das Hilfsverb vor dem Subjekt: did we reduce.
After “Not only” at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: did we reduce.

core: Signalwörter zeigen, wie dein Satz zum vorigen passt: That said = trotzdem, To build on that = darauf aufbauend, Coming back to … = zurück zu …, On the other hand = andererseits, In short = kurz gesagt.

Signal phrases show how your sentence fits the previous one: That said = even so, To build on that = adding to that, Coming back to … = returning to …, On the other hand = in contrast, In short = to sum up.
why: In Meetings und Mails zeigen Diskursmarker, wohin der Gedanke geht. Das wirkt strukturiert und gibt dir Zeit zum Nachdenken, ohne „ähm“.
In meetings and emails, discourse markers show where your thought is going. You sound structured and buy time to think without saying “um”.
contrast: Deutsche nehmen oft „but“ oder „and“ für alles. „That said“ entspricht „Allerdings“, „To build on that“ etwa „Daran anknüpfend“. Achtung: „on the other side“ ist ein Ort, der Gegensatz heißt „on the other hand“.

German speakers often use “but” or “and” for everything. “That said” is close to “Allerdings”, “To build on that” to “Daran anknüpfend”. Careful: “on the other side” is a place; the contrast is “on the other hand”.
steps: Was will ich tun: einschränken, anknüpfen, zurückkommen, gegenüberstellen oder zusammenfassen?
Passenden Marker wählen.
An den Satzanfang stellen, danach ein Komma.
Präposition prüfen: coming back to, build on.
What do I want to do: qualify, build on, return, contrast or sum up?
Choose the matching marker.
Put it at the start, followed by a comma.
Check the preposition: coming back to, build on.
forms: That said, the timeline is still tight.
To build on that, we could add e-invoicing in phase two.
Coming back to your question about pricing, the licenses are per user.
In short, the pilot paid off.

traps.bad: Coming back on your question, the price includes support.
traps.good: Coming back to your question, the price includes support.
why: Es heißt „coming back to“.
The phrase is “coming back to”.

core: Im formellen Englisch wird aus einem Verb oft ein Nomen: „the migration of the data“ statt „we migrated the data“. Nach „following“ und „upon“ steht ein Nomen, kein ganzer Satz: „Following the review, …“
In formal English a verb often becomes a noun: “the migration of the data” instead of “we migrated the data”. After “following” and “upon” you use a noun, not a full clause: “Following the review, …”
why: Nomen bündeln Information und klingen sachlich – ideal für Betreffzeilen, Zusammenfassungen und Mails an Entscheider. Richtig dosiert wirkt das professionell, zu viel davon bürokratisch.
Nouns pack information and sound factual – ideal for subject lines, summaries and emails to decision makers. In the right dose it sounds professional; too much of it sounds bureaucratic.
contrast: Deutsch liebt Nominalstil ohnehin („nach Freigabe des Budgets“). Die Falle ist die Wortform: Deutsche nehmen oft das Verb statt des Nomens („the approve of“). Das englische Nomen hat eigene Endungen: -tion, -al, -ment, -ery.
German loves nominal style anyway. The trap is the word form: German speakers often use the verb instead of the noun (“the approve of”). English nouns have their own endings: -tion, -al, -ment, -ery.
steps: Welche Handlung steckt im Satz? implement, approve, migrate …
Nomen bilden: implementation, approval, migration …
Mit „of“ anschließen: the approval of the budget.
Gegenprobe: Liest sich die Mail noch leicht? Sonst ein Verb zurückholen.
Which action is in the sentence? implement, approve, migrate …
Form the noun: implementation, approval, migration …
Connect with “of”: the approval of the budget.
Check: does the email still read easily? If not, bring back a verb.
forms: The migration of the legacy data took two weeks.
Following the approval of the budget, we will order the licenses.
We expect a significant reduction in storage costs.

traps.bad: Following the approve of the budget, we will order the licenses.
traps.good: Following the approval of the budget, we will order the licenses.
why: Nach „the“ steht das Nomen: approval.
After “the”, use the noun: approval.

core: Mit einem Partizip kürzt du einen Nebensatz ab, wenn beide Teile dasselbe Subjekt haben. Having + 3. Verbform heißt „nachdem … “ („Having read the contract, we signed it.“). Die -ing-Form heißt „während/indem“ („Using OCR, the system …“). Die 3. Verbform allein ist passiv („Stored in Germany, the data …“).

A participle shortens a clause when both parts have the same subject. Having + past participle means “after …” (“Having read the contract, we signed it.”). The -ing form means “while/by …” (“Using OCR, the system …”). The past participle alone is passive (“Stored in Germany, the data …”).
why: Partizipialsätze sparen „After we had …“ und „Because it is …“ und klingen geschliffen – typisch für Berichte, Mails und Präsentationen auf C1-Niveau.
Participle clauses save “After we had …” and “Because it is …” and sound polished – typical of reports, emails and presentations at C1 level.
contrast: Im Deutschen sind solche Konstruktionen selten („Nachdem wir den Vertrag geprüft hatten …“). Die häufigste Falle: Das Subjekt passt nicht. „Having reviewed the offer, the price was too high“ heißt, der Preis hätte das Angebot geprüft.
German rarely uses these structures. The most common trap: the subject doesn't match. “Having reviewed the offer, the price was too high” means the price reviewed the offer.
steps: Haben Neben- und Hauptsatz dasselbe Subjekt? Nur dann verkürzen.
Vorher erledigt? Having + 3. Form.
Gleichzeitig oder Mittel? -ing-Form.
Passiv? Nur die 3. Form.
Do both clauses have the same subject? Only then shorten.
Done before? Having + past participle.
At the same time or a means? The -ing form.
Passive? Just the past participle.
forms: Having reviewed the contract, we signed it.
Using OCR, the system reads every invoice.
Stored in Germany, the data stays GDPR-compliant.
signals: first this, then the main clause

traps.bad: Having review the offer, the CFO asked for a discount.
traps.good: Having reviewed the offer, the CFO asked for a discount.
why: Nach „Having“ steht die 3. Form: reviewed.
After “Having”, use the past participle: reviewed.

core: Genaue Wörter machen deine Aussage klar: by = spätestens bis („by Friday“), until = die ganze Zeit bis („until Friday“), within = innerhalb von („within two days“). Für Mengen: roughly, just under, well over, twice as … as.

Precise words make your statement clear: by = no later than (“by Friday”), until = all the time up to (“until Friday”), within = inside a period (“within two days”). For amounts: roughly, just under, well over, twice as … as.
why: Entscheider wollen Zahlen und Termine, auf die sie sich verlassen können. „Just under 40,000“ oder „by the end of Q3“ klingt kompetent; „some“ und „soon“ klingen nach Ausweichen.
Decision makers want numbers and dates they can rely on. “Just under 40,000” or “by the end of Q3” sounds competent; “some” and “soon” sound evasive.
contrast: Deutsch „bis Freitag“ deckt Frist und Dauer ab. Englisch trennt: „by Friday“ (spätestens Freitag erledigt) und „until Friday“ (läuft bis Freitag). „Zweimal so schnell“ heißt „twice as fast as“, nicht „two times faster as“.

German “bis Freitag” covers both deadline and duration. English separates them: “by Friday” (done by Friday at the latest) and “until Friday” (lasts until Friday). “Twice as fast as”, not “two times faster as”.
steps: Frist oder Dauer? Frist → by, Dauer → until.
Zeitraum ab jetzt? within + Dauer.
Zahl nicht exakt? roughly, just under oder well over.
Vergleich? Dann „twice as … as“ oder „a fraction of“.
Deadline or duration? Deadline → by, duration → until.
A period from now? within + length of time.
Number not exact? roughly, just under or well over.
Comparison? twice as + adjective + as, a fraction of.
forms: roughly / just under / well over + number
Roughly 40% of the invoices arrive as PDFs.
a fraction of / twice as + adjective + as
The cloud version costs a fraction of the old license.
We need your decision by the end of Q3.
We can deliver within two weeks.
signals: at the latest / no later than

traps.bad: We need your feedback until Friday.
traps.good: We need your feedback by Friday.
why: Frist (spätestens) heißt „by“; „until“ beschreibt eine Dauer.
A deadline (at the latest) is “by”; “until” describes a duration.

core: Nach when, as soon as, until, before, after und by the time steht Präsens oder Present Perfect – auch wenn es um die Zukunft geht: „I’ll call you as soon as I arrive.“ (nicht: as soon as I will arrive).

After when, as soon as, until, before, after and by the time you use the present simple or present perfect – even when you talk about the future: “I’ll call you as soon as I arrive.” (not: as soon as I will arrive).
why: Im Zeitsatz steht das Präsens, auch wenn es um die Zukunft geht. Das Deutsche macht es genauso („Wenn ich ankomme, rufe ich an“). Der Fehler kommt vom Reflex „Zukunft = will“, nicht von der Übersetzung. Im Berufsalltag fällt „when I will arrive“ sofort auf.

The time clause takes the present, even when it is about the future. German does the same (“Wenn ich ankomme, rufe ich an”). The mistake comes from the reflex “future = will”, not from translation. At work, “when I will arrive” stands out at once.
contrast: Aufpassen: Sind when und if Fragewörter (Wann? Ob?), steht will: „I don't know when she will arrive.“ Als Zeitwort („sobald“) gilt das Präsens: „I'll call when she arrives.“
Careful: when and if take will when they are question words (When? Whether?): “I don't know when she will arrive.” As time words (= as soon as) they take the present: “I'll call when she arrives.”
steps: Future-Signal erkennen: when, as soon as, until, before, after, by the time.
Den Zeitsatz ins Präsens setzen: „as soon as it arrives“.
Ist die Handlung dann schon abgeschlossen, Present Perfect wählen: „after we have finished“.
„Will“ gehört nur in den Hauptsatz.
Ist when oder if ein Fragewort (nach know, ask, wonder)? Dann steht will: „I wonder when it will be ready.“
Spot the time word: when, as soon as, until, before, after, by the time.
Put the time clause in the present: “as soon as it arrives”.
If the action will already be complete, use present perfect: “after we have finished”.
Will belongs only in the main clause.
Is when or if a question word (after know, ask, wonder)? Then use will: “I wonder when it will be ready.”
forms: when / as soon as + present simple
I'll text you when I get home.
We'll start once everyone has arrived.
By the time + present, will have + participle
By the time you read this, I'll have left.
We won't sign until they send the draft.
know / ask / wonder + when / if + will
I wonder when the update will be ready.

traps.bad: I'll call you when I will arrive at the airport.
traps.good: I'll call you when I arrive at the airport.
why: Nach „when“ steht das Präsens, nicht „will“.
After “when”, use the present, not will.

traps.bad: We'll start as soon as the meeting will be over.
traps.good: We'll start as soon as the meeting is over.
why: Auch nach „as soon as“ steht das Präsens.
After “as soon as” the present is also required.

core: Diese Wörter ersetzen „if“: unless = wenn nicht, as long as / provided that = nur wenn. Danach steht das Präsens: „We’ll start unless it rains.“ Dazu kommen Should you … = falls Sie … (förmlich, ohne if) und But for = „ohne …“ mit Blick zurück. Nicht dazu gehört otherwise: Es heißt „sonst“, beginnt einen neuen Satz und ersetzt kein if.

These words replace “if”: unless = if not, as long as / provided that = only if. After them you use the present: “We’ll start unless it rains.” Also possible: Should you … = if you should … (formal, no if), and But for = “without …” looking back. Otherwise is not one of them: it means “or else”, starts a new sentence and does not replace if.
why: Diese Wörter machen Bedingungen präziser als „if“: Sie zeigen, ob etwas Pflicht, Ausnahme oder Dank ist. Das klingt in Verträgen und Absprachen professionell.
These words make conditions more precise than “if”: they show whether something is a requirement, an exception or a credit. That sounds professional in contracts and agreements.
contrast: „Unless“ hat die Verneinung schon in sich. Deutsche setzen oft ein zweites „not“: „Unless you don't sign“ meint dann das Gegenteil dessen, was gemeint ist.
“Unless” already contains the negation. Germans often add a second “not”: “Unless you don't sign” then says the opposite of what was meant.
steps: Die Bedingung als Wunsch oder Ausnahme erkennen.
Passendes Wort wählen: unless (Ausnahme), as long as / provided that (Bedingung), Should you (förmlich), but for (Dank). Eine Folge ohne if beginnt mit Otherwise (neuer Satz).
Nach unless, as long as, provided that das Präsens verwenden.
Bei „unless“ keine zusätzliche Verneinung setzen.
Decide whether the condition is an exception, a requirement or a credit.
Choose the word: unless (exception), as long as / provided that (requirement), Should you (formal), but for (credit). A result without if starts with Otherwise (new sentence).
Use the present after unless, as long as and provided that.
Do not add a second negation after unless.
forms: We'll cancel unless enough people sign up.
You can leave early provided that you finish the report.
Should you need anything, call me.
Send it today. Otherwise, we can't pay you this month.
But for + noun, would have + participle
But for your help, we would have failed.
signals: on condition that / for as long as
für den Fall, dass (Vorsorge, kein if)

traps.bad: Unless you don't sign today, the offer expires.
traps.good: Unless you sign today, the offer expires.
why: „Unless“ bedeutet schon „wenn nicht“. Eine zweite Verneinung dreht den Sinn um.
“Unless” already means “if not”. A second negation reverses the meaning.

traps.bad: As long as it will not rain, we'll hold the event outside.
traps.good: As long as it doesn't rain, we'll hold the event outside.
why: Nach „as long as“ steht das Präsens, nicht „will“.
After “as long as” use the present, not will.

note: „in case“ ist kein „if“: „Take an umbrella in case it rains“ = für den Fall, dass es regnet (Vorsorge). „If it rains“ ist die Bedingung.
“in case” is not “if”: “Take an umbrella in case it rains” = just in case it rains (precaution). “If it rains” is the condition.
Förmlich geht auch die Umstellung ohne if: Were we to lose the client, … (hypothetisch), Should you need help, … (möglich).
Formally you can also invert without if: Were we to lose the client, … (hypothetical), Should you need help, … (possible).

core: Das Passiv gibt es auch mit Modalverben und in anderen Zeiten: must + be + 3. Verbform („It must be done.“), have been + 3. Verbform („It has been done.“). „is said to …“ und „is believed to …“ sind auch Passiv und heißen „man sagt, dass …“.

The passive also works with modal verbs and other tenses: must + be + past participle (“It must be done.”), have been + past participle (“It has been done.”). “Is said to …” and “is believed to …” are passive too and mean “people say that …”.
why: Im Beruf zählt oft das Ergebnis, nicht die Person: „The invoices must be sent by noon.“ Persönliche Passive wie „is said to“ klingen sachlich und vorsichtig bei Gerüchten.
At work the result often matters more than the person: “The invoices must be sent by noon.” Personal passives like “is said to” sound neutral and careful with rumors.
contrast: Das deutsche „man sagt, dass …“ wird im Englischen gern zu „It is said that …“ oder knapper zu „X is said to …“. Das Passiv mit „werden“ deckt im Englischen mehrere Formen ab.
German “man sagt, dass …” becomes “It is said that …” or, more tightly, “X is said to …”. The German “werden” passive covers several English forms.
steps: Aktiven Satz mit Modal, Perfekt oder -ing erkennen.
Objekt nach vorn, Form von be anpassen: must be / has been / being.
Das Verb als dritte Form (Partizip) setzen: sent, signed, written.
Bei Gerüchten: Subjekt + is said / believed to + Infinitiv (bei Vergangenem to have + Partizip).
Spot the active sentence with a modal, perfect or -ing.
Move the object first and adapt be: must be / has been / being.
Add the past participle: sent, signed, written.
For rumors: subject + is said / believed to + infinitive (for the past, to have + participle).
forms: The files must be sent today.
He is believed to be planning a merger.
signals: must be / has to be + Partizip

traps.bad: The documents must be send to the client by noon.
traps.good: The documents must be sent to the client by noon.
why: Das Passiv braucht das Partizip: „sent“, nicht „send“.
The passive needs the participle: “sent”, not “send”.

traps.bad: Our offer has been accepted yesterday.
traps.good: Our offer was accepted yesterday.
why: Mit „yesterday“ steht die Vergangenheit (was accepted), nicht das Perfekt.
With “yesterday” use the simple past (was accepted), not the perfect.

core: Verben zum Berichten haben feste Strukturen: suggest, recommend, admit, deny + -ing; insist on + -ing; advise, warn + Person + to + Grundform; offer + to + Grundform. Beispiel: „She suggested moving the meeting.“

Reporting verbs follow fixed patterns: suggest, recommend, admit, deny + -ing; insist on + -ing; advise, warn + person + to + base verb; offer + to + base verb. Example: “She suggested moving the meeting.”
why: Im Beruf berichtet man ständig, was jemand empfohlen, zugegeben oder verlangt hat. Das richtige Muster zeigt Präzision und vermeidet typische Fehlkonstruktionen.
At work you constantly report what someone recommended, admitted or demanded. The right pattern shows precision and avoids typical faulty constructions.
contrast: Deutsch erlaubt „Er schlug mir vor, zu gehen“. Englisch sagt nicht „suggested me to go“, sondern „suggested that I go“ oder „suggested going“.
German allows “Er schlug mir vor, zu gehen”. English does not say “suggested me to go”, but “suggested that I go” or “suggested going”.
steps: Das Verb bestimmen: suggest, admit, insist, advise, recommend.
Muster wählen: -ing (suggest, admit, deny), on + -ing (insist), Person + to (advise, warn, tell).
Bei Verneinung: not vor to (not to sign) oder not vor -ing (not signing).
Bei suggest + Person immer einen that-Satz bauen.
Identify the verb: suggest, admit, insist, advise, recommend.
Choose the pattern: -ing (suggest, admit, deny), on + -ing (insist), person + to (advise, warn, tell).
For negatives: not before to (not to sign) or not before -ing (not signing).
With suggest + a person, always build a that-clause.
forms: They insisted on seeing the contract.
She advised us not to wait.

traps.bad: He suggested me to take a different route.
traps.good: He suggested that I take a different route.
why: Nach „suggest“ steht nie „Person + to“, sondern ein that-Satz oder -ing.
After “suggest” there is never “person + to”, but a that-clause or -ing.

traps.bad: She admitted to be late for the meeting.
traps.good: She admitted being late for the meeting.
why: Nach „admit“ steht -ing, kein to-Infinitiv.
After “admit” use -ing, not a to-infinitive.

core: Eine indirekte Frage hat keine Frage-Wortstellung: „Could you tell me where the office is?“ (nicht: where is the office). Ein Frage-Anhängsel sagt das Gegenteil des Satzes: „You’re coming, aren’t you?“ Fragst du nach dem Subjekt, steht kein do: „Who called you?“

An indirect question does not use question word order: “Could you tell me where the office is?” (not: where is the office). A question tag says the opposite of the statement: “You’re coming, aren’t you?” When you ask about the subject, there is no do: “Who called you?”
why: Höfliche Anfragen im Beruf beginnen mit „Could you tell me …“. Dann braucht man normale Satzstellung. Tags laden zur Bestätigung ein und lockern das Gespräch auf.
Polite requests at work start with “Could you tell me …”. This needs normal word order. Tags invite confirmation and relax the conversation.
contrast: Deutsch erlaubt „Weißt du, wo ist das Büro?“ nur umgangssprachlich; Englisch verlangt „where the office is“. Das deutsche „nicht wahr?“ ist im Englischen je nach Satz is it, don't you, shall we.
German allows “Weißt du, wo ist das Büro?” only colloquially; English requires “where the office is”. German “nicht wahr?” varies in English: is it, don't you, shall we.
steps: Direkte Frage in Aussageform umbauen: where the office is.
Mit Could you tell me / Do you know / I wonder einleiten.
Für ja/nein-Fragen if oder whether nutzen.
Beim Tag Hilfsverb und Polarität spiegeln; bei Let's: shall we?
Rebuild the direct question as a statement: where the office is.
Introduce it with Could you tell me / Do you know / I wonder.
For yes/no questions use if or whether.
For tags mirror the auxiliary and flip polarity; after Let's use shall we?
forms: Could you tell me + wh-word + subject + verb
Could you tell me where the meeting is?
I wonder if / whether + subject + verb
I wonder whether the client has replied.
positive statement, negative tag (and vice versa)
You haven't seen my notes, have you?

traps.bad: Can you tell me where is the finance department?
traps.good: Can you tell me where the finance department is?
why: In der indirekten Frage steht das Subjekt vor dem Verb.
In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb.

traps.bad: Who did call me while I was in the meeting?
traps.good: Who called me while I was in the meeting?
why: Bei Fragen nach dem Subjekt steht kein „did“.
In questions about the subject, there is no “did”.

core: should / ought to = Rat, had better = Rat mit Warnung („You’d better hurry.“), must / have to = Pflicht, mustn’t = verboten, don’t have to / needn’t = nicht nötig. Achtung: mustn’t und don’t have to bedeuten etwas ganz anderes.

should / ought to = advice, had better = advice with a warning (“You’d better hurry.”), must / have to = obligation, mustn’t = forbidden, don’t have to / needn’t = not necessary. Careful: mustn’t and don’t have to mean something very different.
why: Die falsche Stärke wirkt im Beruf schnell unhöflich oder unklar. „You must“ klingt wie ein Befehl, „you could“ wie eine Option.
The wrong strength quickly sounds rude or unclear at work. “You must” sounds like an order, “you could” like an option.
contrast: Deutsch nutzt „müssen“ und „sollen“ für fast alles. Aber „mustn't“ ist ein Verbot, „don't have to“ nur „nicht nötig“. Das ist eine häufige Falle.
German uses “müssen” and “sollen” for almost everything. But “mustn't” is a prohibition while “don't have to” only means “not necessary”. That is a common trap.
steps: Entscheiden: Rat, Warnung, Pflicht oder Verbot?
Stärke wählen: could (Option) < should / ought to (Rat) < had better (Warnung) < must (Pflicht).
Nach allen Modalverben steht die Grundform ohne to (außer ought to).
Bei hoher Stellung des Gegenübers abschwächen: Perhaps you could …
Decide: advice, warning, obligation or prohibition?
Choose the strength: could (option) < should / ought to (advice) < had better (warning) < must (obligation).
After all modals use the base form without to (except ought to).
With senior colleagues soften: Perhaps you could …
forms: don't have to / don't need to + base form
You don't have to bring a laptop.

traps.bad: You should to call the client before noon.
traps.good: You should call the client before noon.
why: Nach „should“ steht die Grundform ohne to.
After “should” use the base form without to.

traps.bad: You mustn't come to the meeting if you don't want to; it's optional.
traps.good: You don't have to come to the meeting if you don't want to; it's optional.
why: „Mustn't“ ist ein Verbot. „Nicht nötig“ heißt „don't have to“.
“Mustn't” is a prohibition. “Not necessary” is “don't have to”.

core: Manche Verben brauchen -ing (avoid, mind, look forward to), andere to + Grundform (decide, hope). Bei remember, stop, try und regret ändert sich die Bedeutung mit der Form: „stop smoking“ = aufhören, „stop to smoke“ = anhalten, um zu rauchen.

Some verbs need -ing (avoid, mind, look forward to), others need to + base verb (decide, hope). With remember, stop, try and regret the meaning changes with the form: “stop smoking” = quit, “stop to smoke” = pause in order to smoke.
why: Die falsche Form verändert den Sinn: „I stopped to call“ (ich hielt an) ist etwas anderes als „I stopped calling“ (ich hörte auf). Im Beruf kann das Missverständnisse auslösen.
The wrong form changes the sense: “I stopped to call” (I paused in order to call) differs from “I stopped calling” (I quit). At work that can cause confusion.
contrast: Deutsch hat meist „zu + Infinitiv“. Englisch trennt: „I'm looking forward to meeting you“ (to ist hier eine Präposition), nicht „to meet“.
German mostly uses “zu + Infinitiv”. English separates them: “I'm looking forward to meeting you” (to is a preposition here), not “to meet”.
steps: Verb prüfen: feste -ing-Verben (avoid, mind, enjoy, look forward to) oder feste to-Verben (decide, plan, hope).
Bei remember, stop, try, regret die Bedeutung prüfen.
Vergangenes Erinnern = remember + -ing, Pflicht in der Zukunft = remember + to.
Nach Präpositionen steht immer -ing.
Check the verb: fixed -ing verbs (avoid, mind, enjoy, look forward to) or fixed to-verbs (decide, plan, hope).
With remember, stop, try, regret check the meaning.
Remembering the past = remember + -ing, a future duty = remember + to.
After prepositions always use -ing.
forms: She stopped checking emails on holiday.
Try turning it off and on again.

traps.bad: I'm looking forward to meet you next week.
traps.good: I'm looking forward to meeting you next week.
why: „To“ ist hier eine Präposition, danach folgt -ing.
“To” is a preposition here, so -ing follows.

traps.bad: We decided discussing the budget next week.
traps.good: We decided to discuss the budget next week.
why: Nach „decide“ steht der to-Infinitiv.
After “decide” the to-infinitive is needed.

core: Nach demand, insist, suggest, recommend und it is essential / vital / important that steht die Grundform – ohne -s und ohne Zeitform: „I suggest that he call us.“ (nicht: he calls).
After demand, insist, suggest, recommend and it is essential / vital / important that you use the base form – no -s and no tense: “I suggest that he call us.” (not: he calls).
why: Der Mandativ klingt formell und präzise, besonders in Verträgen, Richtlinien und Berichten. Er zeigt, dass eine Forderung besteht, kein Faktum.
The mandative sounds formal and precise, especially in contracts, policies and reports. It shows a requirement rather than a fact.
contrast: Das Deutsche nutzt Konjunktiv I oder „soll“. Im US-Englisch bleibt das Verb in der Grundform (formell, Standard in Verträgen und Vorschriften); im britischen Englisch steht oft „should“. Beides ist korrekt, aber „that he will resign“ ist hier falsch.

German uses subjunctive I or “soll”. US English keeps the base form (formal, standard in contracts and regulations); British English often uses “should”. Both are correct, but “that he will resign” is wrong here.
steps: Auslöser erkennen: demand, insist, suggest, recommend, essential, vital, important.
Nach „that“ die Grundform setzen: leave, call, be.
Bei Verneinung: not vor dem Verb („that he not sign“), nicht „doesn't“.
Zeitform und -s weglassen: she call, he be.
Spot the trigger: demand, insist, suggest, recommend, essential, vital, important.
After “that” use the base form: leave, call, be.
For negatives: not before the verb (“that he not sign”), not “doesn't”.
Drop tense and -s: she call, he be.
forms: demand / insist / suggest that + subject + base form
It is essential that + subject + be
It is essential that she be present.
He demanded that the report be corrected.
We recommend that he not attend.

traps.bad: The committee demands that he will resign immediately.
traps.good: The committee demands that he resign immediately.
why: Nach „demand that“ steht die Grundform, kein „will“.
After “demand that” use the base form, not “will”.

traps.bad: The board requires that the report will be submitted by Friday.
traps.good: The board requires that the report be submitted by Friday.
why: Nach „require that“ steht in formellem Englisch „be“, kein „will be“.
After “require that” formal English uses “be”, not “will be”.

core: Manche Nomen kann man nicht zählen: advice, information, feedback, equipment. Sie haben keinen Plural und kein „a“: „some advice“, „a piece of advice“. Dazu passen much und a little statt many und a few.
Some nouns cannot be counted: advice, information, feedback, equipment. They have no plural and no “a”: “some advice”, “a piece of advice”. Use much and a little instead of many and a few.
why: Im Deutschen sind „Rat“, „Information“ und „Möbel“ zählbar. Im Englischen sind sie es nicht – das führt zu „advices“ und „informations“.
In German, “Rat”, “Information” and “Möbel” are countable. In English they are not, which leads to “advices” and “informations”.
contrast: Im Deutschen sagt man „ein Rat, zwei Informationen“. Englisch braucht dafür ein Mengenwort: „a piece of advice“.
German says “ein Rat, zwei Informationen”. English needs a unit word: “a piece of advice”.
steps: Ist das Nomen zählbar? Kann ich „two …“ davor sagen?
Wenn nicht: kein „-s“, kein „a/an“, Verb im Singular.
Menge mit „much“, „a little“, „some“ ausdrücken.
Einzelstück: „a piece of …“.
Is the noun countable? Can I say “two …” before it?
If not: no -s, no a/an, singular verb.
Express quantity with much, a little, some.
Single item: “a piece of …”.
forms: Let me give you a piece of advice.

traps.bad: She gave me some good advices.
traps.good: She gave me some good advice.
why: „advice“ hat keinen Plural.
“Advice” has no plural.

traps.bad: The informations are on our website.
traps.good: The information is on our website.
why: „information“ ist unzählbar, das Verb steht im Singular.
“Information” is uncountable, so the verb is singular.

core: Viele Nomen und Adjektive haben eine feste Präposition: reason for, increase in, solution to, interested in, responsible for, good at. Lerne sie zusammen mit dem Wort: „the reason for the delay“.
Many nouns and adjectives have a fixed preposition: reason for, increase in, solution to, interested in, responsible for, good at. Learn them together with the word: “the reason for the delay”.
why: Die falsche Präposition fällt in Berichten und E-Mails sofort auf und wirkt unsicher. Feste Paare sparen Nachdenken.
The wrong preposition stands out in reports and emails and sounds unsure. Fixed pairs save thinking time.
contrast: Deutsch sagt „Lösung für“, „Interesse an“, „gut in“. Englisch: „solution to“, „interested in“, „good at“.
German says “Lösung für”, “Interesse an”, “gut in”. English: “solution to”, “interested in”, “good at”.
steps: Welches Nomen oder Adjektiv steht da?
Feste Präposition aus dem Gedächtnis abrufen, nicht übersetzen.
Nach der Präposition folgt Nomen oder -ing-Form.
Neue Paare immer als Block lernen.
Which noun or adjective is it?
Recall the fixed preposition; don't translate.
A noun or -ing form follows the preposition.
Always learn new pairs as a block.
forms: reason for · increase in · solution to
What is the reason for the delay?
interested in · responsible for · good at

traps.bad: We need a solution of this problem.
traps.good: We need a solution to this problem.
why: Meist „solution to“ + Problem; „solution for“ + Zweck oder Kunde ist auch möglich, „solution of“ ist falsch.
Usually “solution to” + problem; “solution for” + purpose or client is also possible, “solution of” is wrong.

traps.bad: She has a lot of experience on project management.
traps.good: She has a lot of experience in project management.
why: „experience in“ für Fachgebiete.
“Experience in” for fields of work.

core: at + Uhrzeit („at 5“), on + Tag oder Datum („on Monday“), in + Monat oder Jahr („in May“). for + Dauer („for two hours“), since + Beginn („since 9“). by = spätestens, until = bis dahin, within = innerhalb.

at + clock time (“at 5”), on + day or date (“on Monday”), in + month or year (“in May”). for + length of time (“for two hours”), since + starting point (“since 9”). by = no later than, until = up to that point, within = inside a period.
why: Bei Fristen und Terminen entscheidet die Präposition über den Sinn: „by Friday“ und „until Friday“ sind nicht dasselbe.
In deadlines and appointments the preposition changes the meaning: “by Friday” and “until Friday” are not the same.
contrast: Deutsch sagt „seit fünf Jahren“ mit Präsens. Englisch: „for five years“ mit Perfekt: „I have worked here for five years.“
German says “seit fünf Jahren” with the present tense. English uses the perfect: “I have worked here for five years.”
steps: Uhrzeit, Tag oder Monat? at, on oder in wählen.
Dauer („for“) oder Startpunkt („since“)?
Frist („by“), Endpunkt („until“) oder Zeitrahmen („within“)?
Bei „for/since“ meist Present Perfect.
Clock time, day or month? Choose at, on or in.
Duration (for) or starting point (since)?
Deadline (by), end point (until) or time frame (within)?
With for/since, usually the present perfect.
forms: The call is on Monday at 9:30.
We have waited for two weeks.

traps.bad: We have a team meeting at Monday morning.
traps.good: We have a team meeting on Monday morning.
why: Mit Wochentagen steht „on“.
Days take “on”.

traps.bad: I'll be on vacation on August.
traps.good: I'll be on vacation in August.
why: Mit Monaten steht „in“.
Months take “in”.

core: Eine Maßangabe vor dem Nomen steht mit Bindestrich und ohne -s: „a five-minute break“ (nicht: five-minutes). Bei mehreren Adjektiven gilt diese Reihenfolge: Meinung, Größe, Alter, Farbe, Herkunft, Stoff – „a nice old red wooden table“.

A measurement before a noun takes a hyphen and no -s: “a five-minute break” (not: five-minutes). With several adjectives use this order: opinion, size, age, color, origin, material – “a nice old red wooden table”.
why: Wer diese Muster beherrscht, klingt präzise und professionell, besonders in Berichten, Angeboten und Verträgen.
Mastering these patterns sounds precise and professional, especially in reports, offers and contracts.
contrast: Deutsch sagt „ein Bericht mit zehn Seiten“ oder „ein zehnseitiger Bericht“. Englisch: „a 10-page report“ – nie „a 10-pages report“.
German says “ein zehnseitiger Bericht”. English: “a 10-page report” – never “a 10-pages report”.
steps: Steht eine Maßangabe vor dem Nomen? Dann Singular und Bindestrich.
Steht sie nach dem Verb? Dann normal: „The report is 10 pages long.“
Mehrere Adjektive: Meinung vor Größe vor Alter vor Farbe vor Herkunft.
Nach dem Verb „be“ steht kein Bindestrich: „well known“.
Is a measurement before the noun? Singular and hyphen.
After the verb? Normal: “The report is 10 pages long.”
Several adjectives: opinion before size before age before color before origin.
After “be” no hyphen: “well known”.

traps.bad: She presented a five-pages proposal to the board.
traps.good: She presented a five-page proposal to the board.
why: Vor dem Nomen bleibt das Maßnomen im Singular.
Before the noun the measure word stays singular.

traps.bad: They rent a modern small office downtown.
traps.good: They rent a small modern office downtown.
why: Größe steht vor Alter und Stil.
Size comes before age and style.

core: Bei trennbaren Phrasal Verbs steht ein Nomen in der Mitte oder dahinter („pick up the box“ / „pick the box up“). Ein Pronomen steht immer in der Mitte: „pick it up“. Verben mit drei Wörtern bleiben zusammen: „look forward to it“.

With separable phrasal verbs a noun goes in the middle or after the particle (“pick up the box” / “pick the box up”). A pronoun always goes in the middle: “pick it up”. Three-word verbs stay together: “look forward to it”.
why: Phrasal Verbs sind im Berufsalltag allgegenwärtig. Die falsche Stellung klingt sofort unnatürlich.
Phrasal verbs are everywhere at work. The wrong position sounds unnatural immediately.
contrast: Deutsch trennt Verben im Hauptsatz auch („ich rufe an“). Englisch trennt nur bestimmte Verben, und nur das Pronomen erzwingt es.
German also splits verbs in main clauses (“ich rufe an”). English splits only certain verbs, and only a pronoun forces it.
steps: Ist das Verb trennbar? Wörterbuch prüfen.
Ist das Objekt ein Pronomen? Dann in die Mitte: „hand it in“.
Drei-Wort-Verben (put up with, run out of) bleiben zusammen.
Zusammen mit dem Objekt als Block lernen.
Is the verb separable? Check a dictionary.
Is the object a pronoun? Put it in the middle: “hand it in”.
Three-word verbs (put up with, run out of) stay together.
Learn them as a block with the object.
forms: verb + Nomen + Partikel oder verb + Partikel + Nomen
turn down the offer / turn the offer down
signals: up with / out of / look forward to

traps.bad: Your package is at reception, so please pick up it after lunch.
traps.good: Your package is at reception, so please pick it up after lunch.
why: Das Pronomen steht zwischen Verb und Partikel.
The pronoun goes between verb and particle.

traps.bad: I'm looking forward to see you at the conference.
traps.good: I'm looking forward to seeing you at the conference.
why: Nach „look forward to“ folgt eine -ing-Form.
“Look forward to” is followed by an -ing form.

core: Zwischen Verb und Objekt steht kein Adverb: „I like coffee very much.“ (nicht: I like very much coffee). Der Ort kommt vor der Zeit. Nach never, rarely, seldom, hardly, not only und no sooner steht das Hilfsverb vor dem Subjekt: „Rarely have we seen this.“

Do not put an adverb between the verb and its object: “I like coffee very much.” (not: I like very much coffee). Place comes before time. After never, rarely, seldom, hardly, not only and no sooner the auxiliary goes before the subject: “Rarely have we seen this.”
why: Inversion gibt Sätzen Nachdruck und gehört zum gehobenen Stil, etwa in Präsentationen und Berichten.
Inversion adds emphasis and belongs to a formal style, for example in presentations and reports.
contrast: Deutsch erlaubt „Er erklärte klar den Plan“. Englisch trennt Verb und Objekt nicht: „He explained the plan clearly.“
German allows “Er erklärte klar den Plan”. English does not separate verb and object: “He explained the plan clearly.”
steps: Steht ein verneinendes Adverb am Satzanfang? Dann Inversion.
Hilfsverb vor das Subjekt; fehlt eines, „do/does/did“ ergänzen.
Verb und Objekt zusammenlassen, Adverb davor oder dahinter.
Reihenfolge am Satzende: Art und Weise, Ort, Zeit.
Does a negative adverb open the sentence? Use inversion.
Auxiliary before the subject; if there is none, add do/does/did.
Keep verb and object together, adverb before or after.
Order at the end: manner, place, time.
forms: Rarely do we get such feedback.
Not only did … but … / No sooner had … than …
No sooner had we left than it rained.

traps.bad: Rarely we get such positive feedback from clients.
traps.good: Rarely do we get such positive feedback from clients.
why: Nach „rarely“ am Satzanfang folgt Inversion mit „do“.
After sentence-initial “rarely” comes inversion with “do”.

traps.bad: He explained clearly the plan to the team.
traps.good: He explained the plan clearly to the team.
why: Verb und Objekt werden nicht durch ein Adverb getrennt.
A verb and its object are not separated by an adverb.

core: although + ganzer Satz; despite / in spite of + Nomen oder -ing. however, therefore und nevertheless verbinden zwei Sätze: davor Punkt oder Semikolon, danach Komma. whereas und while drücken einen Gegensatz aus.

although + full clause; despite / in spite of + noun or -ing. however, therefore and nevertheless link two sentences: a period or semicolon before, a comma after. whereas and while express a contrast.
why: Richtige Konnektoren machen Argumente logisch und lesbar. Ein falsches Satzzeichen wirkt in E-Mails und Berichten schnell nachlässig.
The right linkers make arguments logical and readable. A wrong punctuation mark looks careless in emails and reports.
contrast: Deutsch sagt „obwohl“ und „trotz“ mit Nebensatz oder Nomen. Englisch: „although + Satz“, aber „despite + Nomen“ – nie „despite we were“.
German has “obwohl” (clause) and “trotz” (noun). English: “although + clause”, but “despite + noun” – never “despite we were”.
steps: Folgt ein ganzer Satz oder ein Nomen? Satz: although. Nomen: despite.
Gegensatz zweier Sätze? Mit „however“ neuen Satz beginnen oder Semikolon.
Folge: „therefore“; Gegensatz trotzdem: „nevertheless“.
Nach „however“ und „therefore“ steht ein Komma.
A full clause or a noun? Clause: although. Noun: despite.
Contrast between two sentences? Start a new sentence with however, or use a semicolon.
Result: therefore; contrast anyway: nevertheless.
A comma follows however and therefore.
forms: despite / in spite of + Nomen oder -ing

traps.bad: Despite we were short on time, we completed the audit.
traps.good: Although we were short on time, we completed the audit.
why: Vor einem ganzen Satz steht „although“, nicht „despite“.
A full clause takes “although”, not “despite”.

traps.bad: In spite the delay, the project was a success.
traps.good: In spite of the delay, the project was a success.
why: „in spite“ braucht immer „of“.
“In spite” always needs “of”.

core: the + Komparativ …, the + Komparativ … heißt „je … desto …“. as + Adjektiv + as heißt „genauso … wie“, Komparativ + than heißt „… als“. far, much und slightly verstärken den Komparativ: „far better“.

the + comparative …, the + comparative … means “the more …, the more …”. as + adjective + as means “just as … as”, comparative + than means “… than”. far, much and slightly modify the comparative: “far better”.
why: Genaue Vergleiche machen Angebote, Berichte und Argumente überzeugend. Ob etwas „far“ oder nur „slightly“ besser ist, ändert die Aussage.
Precise comparisons make offers, reports and arguments convincing. Whether something is far or only slightly better changes the message.
contrast: Deutsch vergleicht mit „als“ und „wie“. Englisch trennt streng: „higher than“, aber „as high as“ – nie „higher as“.
German uses “als” and “wie” for comparisons. English separates them strictly: “higher than”, but “as high as” – never “higher as”.
steps: Gleich oder verschieden? Gleich: as … as, verschieden: Komparativ + than.
Kurze Adjektive: -er; lange Adjektive: more + Adjektiv.
Entwicklung? „The more …, the more …“ mit „the“ vor beiden Teilen.
Stärke mit far/much, Mildern mit slightly/a bit.
Equal or different? Equal: as … as, different: comparative + than.
Short adjectives: -er; long adjectives: more + adjective.
A development? “The more …, the more …” with “the” before both parts.
Strengthen with far/much, soften with slightly/a bit.
forms: This is as fast as that.

traps.bad: This solution is more cheaper than the previous one.
traps.good: This solution is cheaper than the previous one.
why: Kurze Adjektive: „cheaper“, nicht „more cheaper“.
Short adjectives: “cheaper”, not “more cheaper”.

traps.bad: Our sales are higher as last year.
traps.good: Our sales are higher than last year.
why: Nach dem Komparativ steht „than“.
After the comparative comes “than”.

core: Nach einem verneinenden oder einschränkenden Einleiter am Satzanfang steht das Hilfsverb vor dem Subjekt: „Never have we seen such demand.“ Das gilt auch für Only after, No sooner und für Bedingungen ohne if (Should you, Had we).

After a negative or limiting word at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: “Never have we seen such demand.” The same holds for Only after, No sooner and for conditions without if (Should you, Had we).
why: Im Englischen betont man nicht nur mit der Stimme, sondern auch mit dem Satzbau. Die Umstellung macht aus einer Feststellung eine Betonung. Wann ja, wann nein: „Should you need …“ ist in Mails Standard, „Rarely have we seen …“ wirkt im amerikanischen Alltag steif und passt eher in Reden und Berichte.

English stresses not only with the voice but also with sentence structure. Inversion turns a statement into emphasis. When yes, when no: “Should you need …” is standard in emails, “Rarely have we seen …” sounds stiff in everyday American speech and fits speeches and reports better.
contrast: Aufpassen: Mitten im Satz bleibt alles normal („We have rarely seen …“). Nur am Satzanfang kehrt sich die Stellung um. Gibt es kein Hilfsverb, hilft do: „Rarely do we see …“.
Careful: inside the sentence everything stays normal (“We have rarely seen …”). Only at the start does the order flip. If there is no auxiliary, do helps: “Rarely do we see …”.
steps: Steht ein Einleiter wie Never, Rarely, Only after, No sooner vorn?
Gibt es schon ein Hilfsverb? Dann kommt es vor das Subjekt.
Gibt es keines, setze do, does oder did davor.
Bei „No sooner“ folgt than, bei „Hardly“ folgt when.
Does a word like Never, Rarely, Only after or No sooner come first?
Is there an auxiliary already? Then it goes before the subject.
If there is none, add do, does or did.
After “No sooner” comes than, after “Hardly” comes when.
forms: Never / Rarely / Seldom / Little + auxiliary + subject + verb (after have / had: participle, after do / does / did: base form)
Rarely have I seen such a clear proposal.
Only + time or condition + auxiliary + subject + verb
Only after the pilot did we approve the full rollout.
No sooner + had + subject + participle + than + past simple
No sooner had we signed than the prices rose.
Should / Were / Had + subject + …, main clause
Should you need any help, please let us know.

traps.bad: Rarely we have seen such a clear proposal.
traps.good: Rarely have we seen such a clear proposal.
why: Im Deutschen rückt das Verb nach dem ersten Satzglied von selbst an die zweite Stelle. Im Englischen geschieht das nur nach solchen Einleitern, und man vergisst es, wenn der Satz sonst normal läuft.
In German the verb moves to second place on its own after the first element. In English that only happens after words like these, and it is easy to forget when the sentence otherwise runs normally.

traps.bad: Only after the pilot we approved the full rollout.
traps.good: Only after the pilot did we approve the full rollout.
why: Das Deutsche sagt „Erst nach der Pilotphase haben wir …“, dort ist die Umstellung selbstverständlich. Im Englischen fehlt sie leicht, weil „only“ nicht wie ein Verneinungswort wirkt.
German says “Erst nach der Pilotphase haben wir …”, where the inverted order is natural. In English it is easy to miss, because “only” does not look like a negative word.

traps.bad: No sooner had we signed when the prices rose.
traps.good: No sooner had we signed than the prices rose.
why: Zu „no sooner“ gehört „than“, zu „hardly“ und „scarcely“ gehört „when“. Beides wird leicht vertauscht, weil das Deutsche beides mit „als“ oder „da“ wiedergibt.
No sooner goes with than, hardly and scarcely go with when. The two are easily mixed up, because German renders both with “als” or “da”.

traps.bad: Should you will need help, please call us.
traps.good: Should you need help, please call us.
why: Im Deutschen heißt es „Sollten Sie Hilfe brauchen“ in der Gegenwartsform. Auch im Englischen steht nach Should you die Grundform, ohne will, obwohl die Bedingung in die Zukunft zeigt.
German says “Sollten Sie Hilfe brauchen”, and people like to add will because it is about the future. After Should you, though, the base form follows.

core: Vier Wege zur Betonung: do vor der Grundform („I do think“), ein vorangestelltes Adjektiv mit as („Tempting as it is“), So/Such … that mit Umstellung und ein vorgezogenes Objekt („This we must avoid“).
Four ways to stress: do before the base form (“I do think”), a fronted adjective with as (“Tempting as it is”), So/Such … that with inversion and a fronted object (“This we must avoid”).
why: Englisch betont mit der Stimme und mit dem Satzbau: do wird beim Sprechen betont, die anderen Formen ändern die Wortstellung. Wann ja, wann nein: do und Tempting as it is sind im Alltag und in Mails üblich. So … that und Such was … sind gehoben. Das vorgezogene Objekt (This we must avoid) ist selten, lies es zu erkennen, setze es sparsam ein.

English stresses with the voice and with sentence structure: do is stressed in speech, the other forms change the word order. When yes, when no: do and Tempting as it is are common in everyday speech and emails. So … that and Such was … are elevated. The fronted object (This we must avoid) is rare: learn to recognize it and use it sparingly.
contrast: Nicht verwechseln: Nach as bleibt die normale Stellung („as it is“). Nach So/Such am Satzanfang kehrt sie sich um („So fast was …“). Nach do steht immer die Grundform.
Do not mix up: after as the normal order stays (“as it is”). After So/Such at the start it flips (“So fast was …”). After do the base form always follows.
steps: Willst du bestätigen? Setze do/does/did vor die Grundform.
Willst du einräumen? Adjektiv + as + Subjekt + Verb.
Willst du die Folge betonen? So/Such vorn, Verb vor Subjekt, dann that.
Willst du ein Objekt hervorheben? Stelle es vor das Subjekt, ohne Umstellung.
Do you want to confirm? Put do/does/did before the base form.
Do you want to concede? Adjective + as + subject + verb.
Do you want to stress the result? So/Such first, verb before subject, then that.
Do you want to stress an object? Put it before the subject, without inversion.
forms: Subject + do / does / did (stressed) + base form
We did send the invoice last week; please check your spam folder.
Adjective / adverb + as / though + subject + verb, main clause
Tempting as it is, we should not cut the testing phase.
So + adjective + verb + subject + that … / Such + verb + subject + that …
So fast was the rollout that nobody noticed the change.
This we must avoid at all costs.
signals: as it is / as it seems

traps.bad: We did sent the invoice last week.
traps.good: We did send the invoice last week.
why: Nach did steht die Grundform, auch wenn die Aussage in der Vergangenheit liegt. Im Deutschen betont man mit Wörtern wie „wirklich“ oder „doch“. Im Englischen trägt did die Vergangenheit, deshalb folgt die Grundform: did send.
After did the base form follows, even when the statement is in the past. German has no such form, so the past form slips in.

traps.bad: Tempting as is it, we should wait.
traps.good: Tempting as it is, we should wait.
why: Nach as steht die normale Stellung (it is), nicht die Frageform. Man verwechselt es mit der Umstellung nach Never.
After as the normal order (it is) follows, not the question order. It is mixed up with the inversion after Never.

traps.bad: So fast the rollout was that nobody noticed the change.
traps.good: So fast was the rollout that nobody noticed the change.
why: Im Deutschen heißt es „so schnell war der Rollout“, also Verb vor Subjekt. Im Englischen bleibt man leicht bei der normalen Stellung und vergisst die Umstellung.
In German the verb comes before the subject (“so schnell war der Rollout”). In English it is easy to keep the normal order and forget the inversion.

traps.bad: This must we avoid at all costs.
traps.good: This we must avoid at all costs.
why: Im Deutschen steht nach dem vorgezogenen Objekt das Verb: „Das müssen wir vermeiden“. Im Englischen bleibt die Reihenfolge Subjekt vor Verb.
In German the verb follows the fronted object (“Das müssen wir vermeiden”). In English the order subject before verb stays.

core: Englisch lässt Bekanntes weg: so/not nach think und hope, do so statt des Verbs, one(s) statt des Nomens, those of im Vergleich, und am Ende nur to oder das Hilfsverb.
English leaves out what is known: so/not after think and hope, do so instead of the verb, one(s) instead of the noun, those of in a comparison, and only to or the auxiliary at the end.
why: Wiederholungen wirken im Englischen schwerfällig. Wann ja, wann nein: In Gesprächen und Mails ist die Kurzform Standard. In Verträgen und Berichten wiederholt man das Nomen lieber, damit nichts missverstanden wird.
Repetition sounds heavy in English. When yes, when no: in conversation and emails the short form is standard. In contracts and reports it is safer to repeat the noun so that nothing is misunderstood.
contrast: Nicht verwechseln: so ersetzt einen Gedanken (I hope so), do so eine Handlung (please do so), one ein Nomen (the new one). Und to darf am Ende nie fehlen.
Do not mix up: so replaces a thought (I hope so), do so an action (please do so), one a noun (the new one). And to must never be missing at the end.
steps: Was wurde schon gesagt: ein Gedanke, eine Handlung oder ein Nomen?
Gedanke: so oder not. Handlung: do so oder do the same. Nomen: one(s), those of.
Am Satzende steht to oder das Hilfsverb allein, wenn das Verb bekannt ist.
What has been said already: a thought, an action or a noun?
Thought: so or not. Action: do so or do the same. Noun: one(s), those of.
At the end of the sentence, to or the auxiliary alone is left when the verb is known.
forms: so und not statt eines Satzes
so and not instead of a clause
think / hope / expect / suppose / be afraid + so / not
Will the update be ready on Friday? I think so.
do so / do the same / do it replaces an action
The client asked us to review the draft, and we did so on Monday.
Adjective + one(s) / that of / those of instead of a noun
Our old system is slow, but the new one is fast.
Auxiliary or to without a verb at the end
Can you join the call? I'd love to, but I have another meeting.
signals: i think so / i hope so
so und not statt eines Satzes
so and not instead of a clause
i'd love to / i would like to

traps.bad: Is it ready? I hope that not.
traps.good: Is it ready? I hope not.
why: Nach hope steht not direkt: I hope not. Im Deutschen geht „Ich hoffe, dass nicht“, im Englischen ist „hope that not“ nicht üblich, weil not den Gedanken schon ersetzt.
After hope, not follows directly: I hope not. German allows “Ich hoffe, dass nicht”, but “hope that not” is not used in English, because not already replaces the thought.

traps.bad: She signed the contract, and I did same.
traps.good: She signed the contract, and I did the same.
why: Im Deutschen sagt man „ich tat dasselbe“. Im Englischen darf the nicht fehlen: the same.
